notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2023.tlg001.1st1K-gr: ἐξάρτυσις, συναρμογά and ἐπαφά are technical terms whose exact sense is uncertain. The clause 'ἄνευ λέξεως μελισμάτων ὅπου τε' seems disturbed. ἀφυγίαζον is not a known form; taken as 'healed' (ἐξυγίαζον).

nodes.text: Moreover, the whole Pythagorean school practised what was called 'preparation', 'attunement' and 'contact', usefully turning the dispositions of the soul towards the opposite passions by means of certain suitable melodies. For when they were going to bed, they cleansed their minds of the day's disturbances and echoing noises by certain songs and distinctive melodies, and by this prepared for themselves quiet sleep, with few and good dreams; and on rising from bed they again rid themselves of sluggishness and heaviness by songs of a special kind. And there were times when [they used] melodies without words; and they healed certain passions and diseases, as they say, by truly singing charms over them; and it is likely that it was from here somehow that this word 'charm' (epōidē) came into common use. In this way, then, Pythagoras established the correction of human characters and lives through music as something of the greatest benefit.

From this, then, it has become clear that he took over from the Orphics the essence of the gods as defined by number. Through the same numbers he also practised a wonderful foreknowledge, and a worship of the gods according to the numbers, as closely akin [to them] as possible. One might learn this from the following; for some deed must also be offered as proof of what is said. When Abaris was continuing in the sacred rites customary to him, and was procuring through sacrifices the foreknowledge prized by every race of barbarians — especially through sacrifices of birds, for they consider the entrails of such creatures exact for inspection — Pythagoras, not wishing to take away his zeal for the truth, but to provide it to him through some safer means, without blood and slaughter, and especially also because he held the cock to be sacred to the Sun, accomplished for him what is called the 'all-true', composed by arithmetical science.
